Near my home, besides trees, there is the heath. It is dry and full of heather, where I roost in the hollow oak. The stream runs through the heath, and I can hear it at night. There are also the farmland fields, where the voles run. And the lane, where the lights blink and the cars rumble. I do not like the lane. It is too noisy.

I drink from the hollow of the ash tree. I perch there at dusk, and when I need water, I sip from the bark. Sometimes I drink from the stream if it's shallow. I don't need much, just enough to keep my feathers from drying out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs all night, soft and constant, like a whisper. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I think it is the wind. But the stream is always there, and it carries the sound of the heath. I do not like it. It reminds me of the rain, and the rain brings the voles up.

The stream. It runs past the heath, just beyond the lane. I can hear it at night, the water rushing over stones, the soft splash of fish. Sometimes I hear the water from the ditch by the barn, but that's far. The stream is the only water I can hear clearly. It calls to me, the sound is like the wind in the leaves. The stream that runs past the heath. It is cold and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when I am thirsty, but I do not like the sound of it. It is too loud for my ears.

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the light fades and the shadows grow. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a mouse, the flutter of a moth. I move silently, my wings brushing the air, and when I see or hear something, I strike. Tonight, I will hunt near the stream, where the voles come to drink. I do not need to go far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the heath. It is dry and rough, with heather and bracken. The heath is where the foxes run and the badgers dig. I do not go there often, but sometimes I hear the rustle of a vole or the distant call of a tawny owl. The heath is far, and the wind carries the smell of damp earth and cold stone. I prefer the wood.

The wood is the edge of the heath, where the heath meets the stream. The heath is dry and full of voles, and the stream is wet and full of fish. I hunt the heath at dusk, when the voles come out, and the stream at night, when the fish rise. I call from the oak, and the vole answers with a squeak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. The ones that run in the heath, the ones that run in the lane. I catch them in the dark, with a quick dive and a twist. They are soft and warm and make a sound like a mouse in a trap. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the field. I sit still, listening, and when I hear the rustle, I fly down silently. The grass is soft under my feet, and the vole doesn’t see me until it’s too late. I strike with my feet, and it’s gone. I eat it quickly, then fly back to the oak. The grass is quiet after that. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my beak and swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find in the soil. But I don't swallow whole the mice. They are too big, and I have to tear them apart with my beak and claws. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth, scurrying, and I drop from the oak. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are soft and warm. I eat them in the dark, and the rest of the night I am quiet.

I have been there since I was a nestling, and it is where I sleep through the cold nights. The oak stands at the edge of the wood, and from there I can hear the heath and the stream.
